audit_scope.description: Batch 14 covers wallet-application interaction protocols, JavaScript Provider APIs (EIP-2700), and client-side security mechanisms. This batch has significant focus on the boundary between web applications and Ethereum nodes.

in_scope: JSON-RPC provider API exposed to applications

trusted_external_entities.name: Web-based DApps via JavaScript - Provider API Requests
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Web applications (DApps) request access to Ethereum accounts, send transaction requests, and query blockchain state via injected provider (window.ethereum). DApps are untrusted JavaScript code running in browser, potentially malicious or compromised. Provider must enforce user authorization for account access and transaction signing. DApps can request arbitrary data and attempt social engineering to gain excessive permissions.

trusted_external_entities.name: Malicious Web Applications - Phishing and Attack Attempts
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Malicious websites can inject malicious JavaScript, attempt phishing attacks, request excessive permissions, or trick users into signing malicious transactions. Provider must implement permission prompts, transaction simulation/preview, origin validation, and security warnings. Users are the weakest link in authorization decisions.

trusted_external_entities.name: Browser Wallet Extensions - Provider Implementation
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Wallet's JSON-RPC connection to EL node
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Wallet extensions (MetaMask, etc.) mediate between DApps and EL nodes. Wallets implement the provider API and connect to nodes via JSON-RPC. Wallets are semi-trusted as they handle private keys and user authorization, but wallet software could be malicious or compromised. EL node must validate all RPC requests regardless of wallet source. Wallet compromise would leak keys and allow unauthorized transactions.

trusted_external_entities.name: End Users - Authorization Decisions
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Users make authorization decisions (account access, transaction signing) through wallet UI prompts. Users can be socially engineered, make mistakes, or not understand security implications. EL node must assume user authorization may be tricked. Transaction simulation, clear prompts, and security warnings are critical but rely on user comprehension.

boundary_edges.security_assumption: DApp requests account access via eth_requestAccounts. Provider (wallet) must prompt user for permission before exposing any account addresses. DApp origin should be displayed to user. No accounts should be exposed without explicit user approval. Permissions should be revocable by user.

DApp submits unsigned transaction request via eth_sendTransaction. Wallet must display transaction details (to, value, data, gas) to user for approval. User must explicitly authorize signing. Wallet should simulate transaction and warn of dangerous operations (SELFDESTRUCT, token approvals, suspicious contracts). Signed transaction is validated by EL node before inclusion in mempool.

Malicious DApps attempt various attacks: phishing (fake transaction prompts), permission escalation (requesting unnecessary accounts), data harvesting (querying balances), transaction manipulation (hidden parameters in data field). Provider must implement origin isolation, clear transaction display, simulation warnings, and rate limiting. EL node validates all transactions regardless of wallet trust.

Wallet connects to EL node JSON-RPC endpoint (often public or user-configured). RPC connection should use TLS to prevent MITM. Wallet submits user-authorized transactions and queries. EL node must rate-limit RPC calls, validate all transaction signatures and parameters, and not trust wallet-provided data beyond signatures. Compromised wallet can submit arbitrary RPC calls.

User reviews transaction in wallet UI and approves or rejects. UI must clearly display: recipient address, value, gas costs, contract interaction warnings, simulation results. User may not understand technical details, so critical warnings must be prominent. Approved transactions are signed with user's private key. Social engineering can bypass all technical controls if user is tricked into approval.
